source.citation: Turon G, Hlozek J, Woodland JG, Kumar A, Chibale K, Duran-Frigola M. First fully-automated AI/ML virtual screening cascade implemented at a drug discovery centre in Africa. Nat Commun 14, 5736 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41512-2.

edits.text: Data-driven drug discovery remains difficult to streamline, particularly in resource-limited settings. Here, we introduce ZairaChem, an artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) tool for quantitative structure-activity/property relationship (QSAR/QSPR) modelling. ZairaChem is fully automated, has modest computational requirements, and performs robustly across a wide range of datasets. We report its end-to-end implementation at the H3D Centre, Africa's leading integrated drug discovery unit, where no AI/ML capabilities previously existed. Leveraging more than a decade of in-house data, we developed a virtual screening cascade for malaria and tuberculosis drug discovery comprising 15 models of key decision-making assays, spanning whole-cell phenotypic screening, cytotoxicity, aqueous solubility, permeability, microsomal metabolic stability, cytochrome inhibition, and cardiotoxicity. We demonstrate that computational profiling of compounds before synthesis and testing can effectively guide the progression of frontrunner compounds at H3D. To our knowledge, this work represents the first large-scale deployment of AI/ML tools in a research centre operating in a low-resource setting.

edits.anchor: The cost of bringing new medicines
edits.leftover: contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6} in place of the citation [6,7]
edits.text: Drug discovery is a complex, costly, and time-consuming endeavour. The cost of bringing a new medicine to market has risen steadily since the 1970s [1], with recent estimates pointing to a median of $1.3 billion per drug [2] and development timelines averaging 10 years [3]. In response, the pharmaceutical industry has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), and investment in these technologies has surged over the last five years [4]. AI/ML holds the promise of transforming drug discovery from a slow, sequential, high-risk process into a streamlined and integrated pipeline that delivers novel clinical candidates with a lower risk of failure [5]. Notably, AI/ML now plays a pivotal role in quantitative structure-activity/property relationship (QSAR/QSPR) modelling, enhancing predictive performance and offering valuable insights that guide drug design contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}.

edits.anchor: The promise of AI/ML for biomedicine
edits.text: The promise of AI/ML in biomedicine also extends to infectious diseases, which remain underrepresented in drug discovery portfolios [8]. These diseases predominantly affect lower-to-middle-income countries (LMICs), most of which are located in the Global South. Africa, for example, accounts for over 95% of the 240 million annual global cases of malaria [9] and 25% of global deaths from tuberculosis [10]. Historically, efforts to address these challenges have been concentrated in the Global North; as a result, African drug discovery has depended largely on international funding agencies, with programmes driven from abroad. AI/ML methods offer an opportunity to revitalise and accelerate drug discovery projects in low-resource settings. However, limited data science expertise and restricted access to computational resources continue to hinder the adoption of AI/ML at research institutions and universities in LMICs [11]. Lowering these barriers is expected to enable important scientific contributions from the countries that bear a disproportionate burden of infectious diseases, marking a milestone towards their eradication.

edits.anchor: This is the first comprehensive AI/ML-based
edits.text: As far as we know, no other AI/ML-based QSAR/QSPR virtual screening cascade has reached production in a drug discovery setting on the African continent. ZairaChem runs on an ordinary computer and needs no manual tuning, so a team with little data science experience can operate it and retrain the models as new data arrive. Because the cascade rests on in-house data and free, open-source software, we expect it to be a workable starting point for affordable and sustainable drug discovery elsewhere in the Global South.

edits.anchor: Finally, we demonstrate the ability of the ZairaChem pipeline to facilitate transference
edits.text: Finally, we demonstrate that the ZairaChem pipeline can facilitate the transfer of knowledge from literature data to a narrower chemical space. Specifically, models trained on external datasets (P450 CYPs models) perform better when in-house data points are added to the training set. Notably, the AUROC of the two worst-performing models on H3D data (CYP2C19 and CYP2D6) improves upon the inclusion of internal data points (Supplementary Fig. 6).

edits.anchor: We have introduced ZairaChem, a robust and parameter-free
edits.text: We have introduced ZairaChem, a robust, parameter-free AutoML tool that combines a range of chemical descriptors with an ensemble of AI/ML algorithms to train QSAR/QSPR models with SOTA performance out of the box. Automation is essential for the continuous integration and deployment of AI/ML assets in an environment such as H3D, where data science capacity remains limited. We applied ZairaChem systematically to the existing drug discovery pipeline at H3D, yielding 15 production-ready models for key assays in the antimalarial and antitubercular screening cascades. Whether trained on in-house or public data, ZairaChem models performed excellently, with most AUROC scores exceeding 0.75. The resulting hit enrichment reduces attrition in the experimental pipeline and may shorten the bench-to-bedside timeline. For instance, we show that testing just 50 compounds from the whole-cell screening data identifies four times more active compounds against Pf (NF54 strain) and Mtb (H37Rv strain) than testing the same number of randomly selected compounds. This is particularly relevant for research conducted in LMICs, where resources are typically constrained.

edits.text: Certainly! Here is a revised version of the paragraph: Our analysis of individual chemical series sheds light on how model performance evolves as compounds from the same series are incrementally added to the training set. When local data are scarce, model quality varies considerably across series. Notably, approximately 30 local molecules per series emerges as a practical rule of thumb for building models capable of prioritising compound designs for subsequent rounds of synthesis. Additional data, whether local or global, generally enhances performance further.

edits.anchor: Finally, we have demonstrated how AI/ML-aided decision-making
edits.text: Furthermore, by recreating a study performed at H3D in 2020, we have demonstrated that AI/ML-aided decision-making can reduce attrition rates and accelerate project progression during de novo library screening. Representing compounds as colour vectors derived from AI/ML model scores provides an intuitive visual overview, enabling the rapid identification of the most promising candidates: those highly potent against Pf while exhibiting good solubility and low toxicity. We also extended our validation to prospective data from the year following model training. The models proved effective at prioritising novel compounds from active chemical series across two disease areas, underscoring their potential to expedite the discovery of promising drug leads while conserving resources. Overall, the ZairaChem virtual screening cascade empowers scientists to explore a broader chemical space and to make more informed decisions about what to synthesise and test, taking into account predicted assay outcomes that are typically considered only at later stages of a drug discovery programme.

edits.anchor: In conclusion, we have successfully developed and deployed
edits.text: To conclude, we built and deployed an AI/ML-based QSAR/QSPR virtual screening pipeline that depends only on open-source code and conventional computers. Every ZairaChem model pre-trained on H3D data can be downloaded, and lighter versions can be tried in a web-based GUI (https://bit.ly/h3d-app). No virtual screening cascade had previously been built with data produced on the African continent and for it. We offer this work as proof of concept that AI/ML tools can support drug discovery in LMICs, and emerging centres in West Africa [37] and Central Africa [38] could adopt a similar set-up. Beyond Africa, ZairaChem gives anyone modelling small-molecule bioactivity data a free and regularly updated alternative that is competitive with existing tools and can be run without strong data science skills.
